subject: mathematics
question_text: In a △ABC, prove that r₁/(bc) + r₂/(ca) + r₃/(ab) = 1/r − 1/(2R).

mark_split.label: Write one term in half angles
Cancel to a sum of squares

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.
formula_note: Built from the same half-angle forms as the r + r₁ + r₂ − r₃ = 4R cos C family: r = 4R sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2), r₁ = 4R sin(A/2)cos(B/2)cos(C/2), and its rotations. Converting b, c by the sine rule and cancelling turns each term into sin²(half angle)/r, which the half-angle sum identity then finishes.

steps.label: Write one term in half angles
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Substitute r₁ = 4R sin(A/2)cos(B/2)cos(C/2) and b, c by the sine rule, then cancel. Write ONE term with a sigma; the other two follow by symmetry.
steps.memory_tip: Substitute r₁ = 4R sin(A/2)cos(B/2)cos(C/2) and the sine rule for b, c. Write ONE term with a sigma.

recall.must_convey: That r₁ = 4R sin(A/2)cos(B/2)cos(C/2) and b = 2R sinB are substituted, and sinB expanded into half angles.

steps.why: Every quantity in the identity can be written with half angles, so write all of them that way in the first line. The sigma keeps the working to one term instead of three.
common_mistakes: Writing r₁ with cos(A/2) instead of sin(A/2).
Expanding all three terms in full and running out of space.

steps.label: Cancel to a sum of squares
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. The cos(B/2) and cos(C/2) cancel top and bottom, and what is left has sin(A/2) over 4R sin(B/2)sin(C/2) — which becomes sin²(A/2)/r.
steps.memory_tip: The cos(B/2) and cos(C/2) cancel; multiplying top and bottom by sin(A/2) turns what is left into sin²(A/2)/r.

recall.must_convey: That the cosines cancel and the denominator becomes r = 4R sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2), leaving (1/r)Σsin²(A/2).

steps.why: Multiplying top and bottom by sin(A/2) makes the denominator 4R sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2), which equals r.
common_mistakes: Cancelling the sines rather than the cosines.
Not spotting that the denominator is r.

steps.label: Use the half-angle sum identity
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) = 1 − 2 sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) — the Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations identity, quoted.
steps.memory_tip: Σsin²(A/2) = 1 − 2 sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2), and that product is r/(4R).

recall.must_convey: That the Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations identity Σsin²(A/2) = 1 − 2sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) is quoted, and the product replaced by r/(4R).

steps.why: This is exactly the identity Σsin²(A/2) = 1 − 2 sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2), proved in the Trigonometric Ratios chapter and quoted rather than re-proved — and r = 4R sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) rearranges to give the product directly.

steps.label: Expand and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Multiply the 1/r through the bracket; the r in the second term cancels, leaving 1/(2R).
steps.memory_tip: Multiply the 1/r through: the r in the second term cancels, leaving 1/(2R).

recall.must_convey: That multiplying out gives 1/r − 1/(2R), with the r cancelling in the second term.
accept: multiply through and the r cancels in the second term leaving one over r minus one over two R

steps.why: The r cancelling in the second term is what leaves a pure 1/(2R) with no r in it — which is exactly the form the question asked for.
common_mistakes: Cancelling the r in the wrong term.

insider_note: Convert everything to half angles and cancel, which turns the sum into (1/r)Σsin²(A/2). The identity Σsin²(A/2) = 1 − 2sin(A/2)sin(B/2)sin(C/2) is what produces the 1/(2R).
